en: Rainwater erodes the coral limestone of Bohol over thousands of years, leaving behind the distinct conical shapes of the Chocolate Hills.
The massive Sierra Madre mountain range forces incoming Pacific typhoons to release their moisture, reducing wind strength before reaching central Luzon.
When cold lake water seeps into Taal Volcano's hot magma chamber, it instantly flashes into steam, causing explosive phreatic eruptions.
Slightly acidic rainwater slowly dissolves the underground limestone of Palawan, carving out the massive caverns of the Puerto Princesa Subterranean River.
The dense, tangled roots of mangrove trees in Pambujan Bay trap moving sediment, which physically blocks waves and prevents coastal erosion.
Deep underground heat in Albay boils groundwater into high-pressure steam, which is piped up to spin turbines and generate electricity at the Tiwi plant.
During high tide, the rising water level of Manila Bay pushes saltwater backward into the Pasig River, temporarily reversing its natural flow.
Repeated, highly viscous lava flows and falling ash from Mayon Volcano cool and stack evenly, building its famous steep, symmetrical cone shape.
Moist winds from the South China Sea hit the Zambales Mountains during the Habagat monsoon, forcing the air upward to drop heavy rain.
Tiny coral polyps in the Sulu Sea extract calcium from seawater to build hard skeletons, slowly forming the massive atolls of Tubbataha Reefs.
Heavy rains wash loose soil from surrounding mountains into Laguna de Bay, where the sediment settles at the bottom and gradually shallows the lake.
Strong ocean currents squeeze through the narrow Verde Island Passage, mixing nutrient-rich waters that feed the plankton supporting its highly diverse coral reefs.
